'''Ephraim Y. Levin''', (February 22, 1933, [[Baltimore, Maryland]], - November 20, 2020) was an American scientist.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-12-02 |title=Ephraim Levin |url=https://www.washingtonjewishweek.com/72711/ephraim-levin/obits/ |access-date=2021-01-20 |website=Washington Jewish Week |language=en-US}}{{dead link|date=April 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Ephraim Levin |url=https://www.sagelbloomfield.com/obituary/Ephraim-Levin |publisher=Sagel Bloomfield Danzansky Goldberg Funeral Care Inc |access-date=12 August 2021}}</ref>

== Academic career ==
1957 BA and MA, 1953, MD, 1957 at [[Johns Hopkins University]]. He had an internship and residencies at [[Johns Hopkins Hospital]] and [[Sinai Hospital (Maryland)|Sinai Hospital of Baltimore.]] He served in the [[United States Public Health Service]] USPHS from 1953 to 1998, and was on active duty from 1958 to 1960 and 1974–1998.{{Citation needed|date=April 2024}}

Along with [[Seymour Kaufman]] he discovered the role of ascorbic acid in the enzymatic hydroxylation of dopamine to form norepinephrine, the first evidence for a specific metabolic function for this vitamin<ref>{{cite journal |last1=LEVIN |first1=EY |last2=LEVENBERG |first2=B |last3=KAUFMAN |first3=S |title=The enzymatic conversion of 3,4-dihydroxyphenylethylamine to norepinephrine. |journal=The Journal of Biological Chemistry |date=July 1960 |volume=235 |issue=7 |pages=2080–6 |doi=10.1016/S0021-9258(18)69366-4 |pmid=14416204|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Fellowship with [[Konrad Emil Bloch|Konrad Bloch]] at [[Harvard University]] 1961–1963, under the auspices of Sinai Hospital.{{Citation needed|date=April 2024}}

He was on the Faculty of Pediatrics at [[Johns Hopkins School of Medicine]] 1963–1974.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20090512082035/http://profiles.nlm.nih.gov/JQ/B/B/J/C/_/jqbbjc.pdf Johns Hopkins University, Programs in Human Genetics]</ref>

Along with [[Vagn F. Flyger|Vagn Flyger]], he demonstrated the partial deficiency of uroporphyrinogen cosynthetase in congenital erythropoietic porphyria of cattle and human beings, its occurrence in asymptomatic carriers of the disease, in fibroblasts as well as in bone marrow, and its probable cause of red bones in fox squirrels.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Levin |first1=Ephraim Y. |last2=Flyger |first2=Vagn |title=Uroporphyrinogen III Cosynthetase Activity in the Fox Squirrel ( Sciurus niger ) |journal=Science |date=October 1971 |volume=174 |issue=4004 |pages=59–60 |doi=10.1126/science.174.4004.59|pmid=5120867 |bibcode=1971Sci...174...59L |s2cid=26381717 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Romeo |first1=Giovanni |last2=Levin |first2=Ephraim Y. |title=Uroporphyrinogen III Cosynthetase in Human Congenital Erythropoietic Porphyria |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |date=July 1969 |volume=63 |issue=3 |pages=856–863 |doi=10.1073/pnas.63.3.856|pmid=5259767 |pmc=223531 |doi-access=free |bibcode=1969PNAS...63..856R }}</ref>

He once beat [[Solomon W. Golomb|Solomon Golumb]] in a chess game.{{Citation needed|date=April 2024}}

== Personal life ==
He married Ruth Lee Shefferman on June 17, 1956, and had four children: Joshua, Rebecca, Daniel, and Michael.<ref>{{Cite web |title=EPHRAIM LEVIN Obituary (2020) - Rockville, DC - The Washington Post |url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/washingtonpost/name/ephraim-levin-obituary?id=6117921 |access-date=2024-06-25 |website=Legacy.com}}</ref>
